member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.CubicSpline
member.summary: Represents a cubic spline curve.

remarks.para: Use the class to interpolate tabulated data, or to approximate a function defined in terms of tabulated data.
A cubic spline is a piecewise curve defined by a third degree polynomial on each interval.

Splines are defined by the data points and some additional conditions. Depending on the nature of these conditions, different types of spline curves arise. There are four kinds of splines. These types are enumerated by the type.

A natural spline is a spline curve whose second derivative at the end points are zero. This type of spline tends to minimize the overall curvature of the spline. There is only one natural spline for a given set of data points.

A clamped spline is a spline curve whose slope is fixed at both end points. There is a clamped spline curve for each pair of slopes. Therefore, two parameters must be defined in addition to the data points to specify a clamped spline completely.
Clamped and natural splines have continuous second derivatives.

A cubic Hermite spline is a spline curve whose slope is fixed at each data point. These slopes must be provided by the user. As a result of these additional conditions, the second derivative is no longer continuous.

An Akima spline is a variation of a spline that is robust against outliers. The polynomial on each interval is defined using only a limited number of points. This means that, unlike natural and clamped splines, the effect of an anomalous data point doesn't propagate throughout the curve. Akima splines require only the data points. No other information is needed.
A smoothing spline is a variation of a natural spline that reduces the curvature of the curve at the expense of no longer interpolating the data points.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.Curve
member.summary: Represents a curve in two-dimensional space.

remarks.para: The class is the base class for classes that represent curves in two-dimensional space. It defines common properties and methods for all such classes. Derived classes provide implementations for specific types of curves.
The name 'Curve' was chosen as an alternative to 'Function', which is a reserved word in many languages.

The method evaluates the curve at a specific point. evaluates the derivative, and evaluates the definite integral over a specified interval. If overridden by a descendant class, the method returns the that is the derivative of the instance. The method attempts to find all the roots or zeros of the curve.

A particular type of curve is defined by a set of parameters. These parameters can be set and retrieved through the property which is a vector. The number of such parameters is given by the property of the property.

is an abstract base class and cannot be instantiated directly. The following derived classes have been defined: ClassDescription
A curve whose value and optionally its derivative is calculated using a function of one variable delegate.
A linear combination of an arbitrary set of curves.
Abstract base class for classes that implement different types of polynomials. Derives from .
A polynomial. Derives from .
A linear combination of Chebyshev polynomials. Derives from .
A natural or clamped cubic spline. Derives from .
A curve that is non-linear in its parameters and is suitable for non-linear curve fitting.
Exponential.
Notes to inheritors: When you derive from , you must override the following member: . You should also override the following members: , , , and .

remarks.para: Use the class to refer to classes that implement curve fitting algorithms. This is an abstract class and cannot be instantiated. Instead, use one of the derived classes: and .
The curve is specified by the property. The data is supplied as objects through the and properties.
The method performs the actual curve fit. This method returns the that best fits the supplied data.

By default, the observations are unweighted. You can supply a weighting method in two ways. You can set the property to a function of two variables delegate that computes the weight for each observation. The class provides predefined delegates for the most common weight functions. Alternatively, you can set the individual weights by setting the property to a that contains the weight for each individual observation.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.FunctionBasis
member.summary: Serves as an abstract base class for collections of functions.

remarks.para: A represents a collection of real functions of one real variable. The class implements a that is a linear combination of basis functions in a .

A function basis is particularly useful for representing a class of functions where the cost of evaluating a series of functions is much less than that of evaluating the functions individually. For example, to evaluate all powers up to degree 10 requires up to 55 multiplications, where only 10 multiplications are required if they are evaluated as a group.

The and methods evaluate all basis functions for a given value or set of values. The and methods evaluate the derivative of all basis functions for a given value or set of values. Derived classes provide optimized implementations of these methods for specific classes of curves.
The curves in a function basis can be combined into a curve using the method. The methods calculate the that is the least squares fit to a set of data points using curves from the function basis.

This is an abstract base class. The following classes derive from : ClassBasis functions
Arbitrary user-defined functions.
Polynomials up to a specified degree.
Chebyshev polynomials over a specified interval up to a specified degree..

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.GeneralCurve
member.summary: Represents a curve in two-dimensional space whose value is defined by a function of one variable delegate.

remarks.para: This class inherits from the class, which provides common properties and methods for all classes that represent two-dimensional curves.

The method evaluates the curve at a specific point. evaluates the derivative, and evaluates the definite integral over a specified interval. If overridden by a descendant class, the method returns the that is the derivative of the instance. The method attempts to find one zero of the function using Newton's method.
Curves of this type do not have any parameters. The collection is always empty.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.LinearCurveFitter
member.summary: Represents an algorithm that calculates a linear least squares fit of a curve.

remarks.para: Use the class to fit data to a curve by the method of least squares. The curve is specified by the property. The parameters of this curve are modified to produce the best fit. The curve must be of a type that inherits from , This includes instances of and .
The data is supplied as objects through the and properties.

By default, the observations are unweighted. You can supply a weighting method in two ways. You can set the property to a function of two variables delegate that computes the weight for each observation. The class provides predefined delegates for the most common weight functions. Alternatively, you can set the individual weights by setting the property to a that contains the weight for each individual observation.
The method performs the actual curve fit. By default, a QR decomposition is used. You can change the default behavior by setting the property to one of the values.

member.summary: Represents a that can be used for a non-linear regression calculation.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent a curve suitable for use in a non-linear curve fitting. The class works only with curves that derive from . See this class for details on how to perform a least squares fit.
is an abstract class and cannot be instantiated directly. Instead, derive your own class from , or use one of the predefined classes listed in the following table:

item.description: A sum of exponential terms.
A standard 4-parameter logistic curve.
A 5-parameter logistic curve that includes an asymmetry factor.
A 4-parameter Gaussian 'bell' curve.
A 4-parameter Lorentz peak curve.
A quotient of two polynomials.
A 4-parameter periodic curve.

remarks.para: Note to inheritors: You must override the method. If possible, you should also override the and methods. By default, a numerical approximation is used as the derivative.

If the difference is significantly greater, then most likely the direct calculation of the partial derivatives contains an error.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.NonlinearCurveFitter
member.summary: Represents an algorithm that fits a nonlinear curve to data.

remarks.para: Use the class to fit data to a nonlinear curve by the method of least squares. The curve, which must be of a type that inherits from , is specified by the property. The data is supplied as objects through the and properties.

The method performs the actual curve fit. This method returns the that best fits the supplied data. The property returns the object that was used to find the least squares solution. To verify that the algorithm terminated normally, you can inspect the 's property, which is of type . A value of Normal indicates that the algorithm terminated normally. However, it is still possible that the algorithm didn't converge to the actual best fit. A visual inspection is always recommended.
The parameters of the fitted curve can be retrieved through the property. The standard deviations associated with each parameter are available through the method.

By default, the observations are unweighted. You can supply a weighting method in two ways. You can set the property to a function of two variables delegate that computes the weight for each observation. The class provides predefined delegates for the most common weight functions. Alternatively, you can set the individual weights by setting the property to a that contains the weight for each individual observation.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.PiecewiseConstantCurve
member.summary: Represents a curve that has different constant values on different intervals within its domain.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent a curve or function whose value is constant over a number of subintervals, but may be different on different intervals.

Piecewise constant curves are defined to be left-continuous. This means that on each interval, the function value at the left or lower bound is equal to the constant value over the interval. The function value at the right or upper bound is equal to the value of the curve on the next interval.
Piecewise linear curves inherit from .

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.Polynomial
member.summary: Represents a polynomial.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent ordinary polynomials. A polynomial is an algebraic expression consisting of one or more summed terms, each term consisting of a constant multiplier and a variable raised to an integral exponent. It inherits from and provides specialized implementation for most methods.
The parameters of a correspond to the coefficients of the polynomial. The coefficients can be accessed through the indexed property. In C#, this property is the indexer for this class.

The method returns the value of the polynomial at a specific point. returns the derivative.
evaluates the definite integral over a specified interval.

The method attempts to find all real roots of the polynomial. It returns a array. The corresponding method attempts to find all complex roots, and returns them as an array of complex number values. The roots are sorted in order of ascending real part.
Methods for arithmetic operations on polynomials have been defined. Corresponding operator overloads are available for those languages that support them.

member.summary: Serves as an abstract base class for derived classes that represent polynomials.

remarks.para: This base class is provided to make it easier for implementers to create classes that implement linear combinations of specific types of univariate polynomials.
This is an abstract base class and cannot be instantiated directly. Instead, create an instance of one of the defined derived classes, or create a class that inherits from .

The following derived classes have been defined: ClassDescription
PolynomialOrdinary polynomials.

Note to inheritors: When you inherit from , you should create a corresponding class that inherits from . In addition, you must override the following members: , , . You may also want to override and .

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.Curves.Nonlinear.RationalCurve
member.summary: Represents a curve that is a quotient of two polynomials.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent a rational function that can be used in non-linear least squares fitting.

A rational curve is a quotient of two polynomials. The degree of the polynomials must be specified when the curve is constructed. A rational curve has n+d+1 parameters, where n is the degree of the polynomial in the numerator, and d is the degree of the polynomial in the denominator. The first n+1 parameters are the coefficients of the polynomial in the numerator, starting with the constant term. The remaining d parameters are the coefficients of the polynomial in the denominator, starting with the linear term. The polynomial in the denominator always has constant term 1.
For details on how to fit a curve of this type, see the class.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.BoundaryIntervalBehavior
member.summary: Enumerates how segments at the boundaries of subdivided series are handled.

remarks.para: The CompleteAndInclude value is used most often with time-related data. For example, if monthly data is requested, but the first interval does not cover an entire month, specifying CompleteAndInclude for the start behavior would indicate the entire first month should be included.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.BoundaryIntervalBehavior.CompleteAndInclude
member.summary: The interval is extended to a full larger interval and the extended interval is included.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.BoundaryIntervalBehavior.Exclude
member.summary: The entire interval is excluded.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.BoundaryIntervalBehavior.Include
member.summary: The interval is included.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.CategoricalEncoding
member.summary: Represents an encoding of the levels in a categorical variable.

remarks.para: Use the class to specify how a categorical variable should be encoded as indicator variables. An encoding is a set of mappings from categories to real numbers. The mappings are returned as objects.

Encodings can have two forms: full rank and reduced rank. A full rank encoding means that, when the encoding is applied to each category, the resulting matrix has full rank. Reduced rank encoding means that the resulting matrix does not have full rank. This is useful when specifying models that include a constant term. In such cases, the full rank encoding and the constant term are linearly dependent.
To create an encoding, use one of the methods of the class. You can then use the or to get the encoding. Alternatively, you can inherit from

The creation of indicator variables is mostly transparent. To create an indicator variable, use the index with the
method.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.DataFrame`2
member.summary: Represents a data frame with row and column indexes of the specified type.
member.typeparam: The element type of the row index.
The element type of the column index.

remarks.para: Use the type to represent a 2-dimensional collection of possibly heterogeneous data. The rows and columns are indexed by keys of type and , respectively. Rows and columns can be accessed through their keys or ordinal position.

Any operation that changes the rows of a data frame always returns a new data frame. Columns can be added and removed from a data frame without creating a new data frame. The values in a column are immutable, so direct modification of data values is not supported.

The columns of a data frame are stored as strongly typed vectors. However, the column types are not part of the type definition of the data frame. This means that the element type of the column must be specified when accessing a column, or an untyped vector is returned as an object. Some care must be taken to specify the correct element type, or an exception may be thrown at runtime.

The fact that the data is stored in columns means that accessing the data is most efficient column-wise. When computing values based on multiple columns, it is better to write the operation in terms of the column vectors than to iterate through the rows of the data frame.

The data frame class supports many data manipulation and transformation operations, including adding and removing columns, selecting rows, structural operations like stacking and creating pivot tables, processing missing values and aggregation. By including the namespace, LINQ queries are also supported.
Hierarchical row and column indexes are supported. In order to return the proper type of the indexes, some structural operations are defined as extension methods in the static class.

member.summary: Use the default action, . The value or row containing the missing value is discarded.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.MissingValueAction.Discard
member.summary: This is the default.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.MissingValueAction.Fail
member.summary: When a missing value is encountered, a is thrown.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.MissingValueAction.Ignore
member.summary: Same as Nothing. No action is taken and the value is ignored. If NaN's are present, Most operations on numerical variables will give as a result.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.MissingValueAction.Nothing
member.summary: Same as Ignore. No action is taken and the value is ignored. If missing values are present, most operations will give a missing value as a result.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.MissingValueAction.ReplaceWithNext
member.summary: Any missing values are replaced with the value of the next observation. If the last observation is missing, it is replaced with 0.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.MissingValueAction.ReplaceWithPrevious
member.summary: Any missing values are replaced with the value of the previous observation. If the first observation is missing, it is replaced with 0.

member.name: F:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.MissingValueAction.ReplaceWithValue
member.summary: Any missing values are replaced with the user-specified value.

member.summary: Represents a statistical model.

remarks.para: This is an abstract base class and cannot be instantiated directly. Instead, use one of the inherited types, as listed in the table below:

item.description: A simple linear regression model with one independent variable.
A regression model with multiple independent variables.
A linear regression model that uses a polynomial in one variable.
A multiple linear regression model with multiple independent variables.
A multiple linear regression model with multiple independent variables.

remarks.para: Note to inheritors: When you inherit from ,you must override .

member.name: P:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.Models.RegressionModel`1.AdjustedRSquared
member.summary: Gets the adjusted R Squared value for the regression.
member.value: The adjusted R Squared value for the regression.

remarks.para: The adjusted R2 value indicates the ratio of variation that is explained by the model to the total variation in the model, adjusted downward to compensate for overfitting.

The larger the number of independent variables is compared to the number of observations, the lower the adjusted R2 value will be. When using models with a larger set of independent variables, the additional variables may be essentially modeling noise.
The unadjusted R2 value is returned by the property.

exception.para: The property is accessed before the model has been computed.

member.value: The that summarizes the results of this model.

exception.para: The property is accessed before the model has been computed.

member.summary: Returns whether another is nested within this instance.
member.param: A object.
member.returns: if is nested within this model; otherwise .

remarks.para: A model is nested within another model if all independent variables used in the nested model are also used in the parent model. If the parent model has an intercept, then the nested model must also have an intercept.

member.name: P:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.Models.RegressionModel`1.FStatistic
member.summary: Gets the F statistic for the regression.

remarks.para: This property returns the value of the F statistic, which gives an indication of the significance of the model. It compares the variance attributed to the model with the variance of the residual. The property returns the P-value corresponding to the F statistic.

member.name: P:Numerics.NET.DataAnalysis.Models.RegressionModel`1.RSquared
member.summary: Gets the R Squared value for the regression.
member.value: The R Squared value for the regression.

remarks.para: The R2 value indicates the ratio of variation that is explained by the model to the total variation in the model. Its value is always between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates the model explains nothing, and 1 means the model explains the data perfectly.

Note that in most situations, irreducible errors in measurement will prevent the model from explaing all the variation. Models using a larger set of factors may produce an R2 value that is closer to 1. However, it may be that the additional factors are essentially modeling noise.
The property returns the adjusted R2 value, which is a somewhat better indicator of goodness of fit.

exception.para: The property is accessed before the model has been computed.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.EquationSolvers.BisectionSolver
member.summary: Represents a that uses the bisection algorithm.

remarks.para: Use the class to solve a simple non-linear equation if you have an interval that includes a root with certainty, and when you only need a rough approximation of the root. If you need higher accuracy, other algorithms are more efficient. TOMS algorithm 748 is the method of choice for these situations.

inherits from , which in turn inherits from . All properties of are available. The and properties set the desired precision as specified by the property. The default value for both tolerances is (roughly 10-8). sets the maximum number of iterations.

The property is a function of one variable that specifies the function we want to find a root for. The and
properties specify the bounds of the bracketing interval. The target function must have a different sign at each end of this interval.

The method performs the actual approximation of the root. This method returns the best approximation that was found. The property indicates whether the algorithm was successful. The property gives an upper bound for the difference between the approximated and the actual root.

The bisection method is the simplest of the root bracketing algorithms. It works by dividing the bracketing interval into two equal parts in each iteration. Not taking into account round-off error, the number of iterations needed to achieve a certain accuracy can be estimated easily as the base 2 logarithm of the relative accuracy. It takes about 10 iterations to gain three digits in accuracy.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.EquationSolvers.DekkerBrentSolver
member.summary: Represents a root finder that uses Dekker and Brent's algorithm.

remarks.para: Use the class to find a root of a function if you have an interval that includes a root with certainty. This is one of the more robust of the root bracketing solver algorithms. The , based on TOMS algorithm 748, is generally somewhat faster and more reliable.

inherits from , which in turn inherits from . All properties of are available. The and properties set the desired precision as specified by the property. The default value for both tolerances is (roughly 10-8). sets the maximum number of iterations.

The property is a function of one variable that specifies the function we want to find a root for. The and
properties specify the bounds of the bracketing interval. The target function must have a different sign at each end of this interval.

The method performs the actual approximation of the root. This method returns the best approximation that was found. The property indicates whether the algorithm was successful. The property gives an upper bound for the difference between the approximated and the actual root.

The Dekker-Brent method is the most advanced of the root bracketing algorithms. It combines the robustness of the bisection method with the increased speed of the regula falsi (false positioning) method.

At each iteration, either a bisection or a regula falsi step is taken, depending on the behavior of the algorithm up to that point. As a result, the Dekker-Brent method will converge as fast as the best case regula falsi method at its best, and as slow as the bisection method at its worst.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.EquationSolvers.DoglegSystemSolver
member.summary: Represents an algorithm that solves a system of nonlinear equations using Powell's dogleg method.

remarks.para: Use the class to solve a system of nonlinear equations. The class uses a variant of Powell's dogleg method to find a solution. This is the method of choice for most problems.

The target functions are set in one of two ways. The property is a delegate that represents a multivariate function returning a vector in its second argument. This is a function that returns a vector containing the values each target function. Alternatively, the method can be used to provide the target functions as an array of multivariate function delegates.

Similarly, the gradients of the target functions can be set in two ways. The property is a delegate that represents a multivariate function returning a matrix in its second argument that calculates the Jacobian of the system of equations. The Jacobian is a matrix whose rows are the gradients of the target functions. Alternatively, the method lets you supply the gradients of individual target functions as an array of either multivariate function returning a vector or multivariate function returning a vector in its second argument delegates.

The starting point for the iteration is set through the property. This property must be set to a valid before the algorithm is run. sets the maximum number of iterations, while sets the maximum number of function evaluations.

The method performs the actual approximation of the root. This method returns the that is best approximation that was found. The property indicates whether the algorithm was successful. One value to look out for is ConvergedToFalseSolution. This occurs when the algorithm converges to a local minimum of the sum of squares of the function valuies.

The algorithm has two convergence tests. By default, the algorithm terminates when either of these is satisfied. You can deactivate either test by setting its property to . If both tests are deactivated, then the algorithm always terminates when the maximum number of iterations or function evaluations is reached.

The first test is based on the uncertainty in the location of the approximate solution. The property returns a object that allows you to specify the desired and specific . See the class for details on how to further customize this test.

The second test is based on the value of the target functions at the approximate solution. The property returns a object that can be used to customize the test. By default, the error is set to the component with the largest absolute value.

The method uses derivative information if it is available. If the property is , and no gradient functions have been supplied, then numerical derivatives are used. Special techniques are used to keep the number of numerical derivative evaluations down to a minimum. Even though the algorithm without derivatives takes less time per iteration, it usually requires significantly more iterations to find a solution. Except for very large problems, or when the evaluation of derivatives is very expensive, derivative information should be supplied.

The dogleg algorithm works by minimizing the sum of the squares of the target functions. The approximation to the solution is updated in each step by either a Newton step, a steepest descent step, or a combination of both.

This method produces excellent results in most cases. However, because the algorithm is in essence a minimizer, it is possible that the algorithm gets 'stuck' in a local minimum, and converges to a point that is not a solution of the system of equations. The property indicates whether an actual solution was found.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.EquationSolvers.HalleySolver
member.summary: Represents a root finder based on Halley's algorithm.

remarks.para: Halley's algorithm starts from a single starting value. It then uses the derivative and second derivative of the target function to find successive approximations of the root.
Halley's method has cubic convergence. This means that once an approximation is close to a root, the number of correct digits will roughly triple in each iteration.

Halley's method therefore has superior convergence properties relative to Newton's method. However, this comes at a cost which is only justified if the second derivative is relatively cheap to compute. One example of this is functions that satisfy differential equations, like the Bessel functions.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.EquationSolvers.NewtonRaphsonSystemSolver
member.summary: Represents a root finder based on the Newton-Raphson algorithm.

remarks.para: Use the class to solve a system of nonlinear equations using the Newton-Raphson method in multiple dimensions. This algorithm is suitable for 'easy' target functions. For most general applications, the class offers a more reliable solution.

The target functions are set in one of two ways. The property is a delegate that represents a multivariate function returning a vector in its second argument. This is a function that returns a vector containing the values each target function. Alternatively, the method can be used to provide the target functions as an array of multivariate function delegates.

Similarly, the gradients of the target functions can be set in two ways. The property is a delegate that represents a multivariate function returning a matrix in its second argument that calculates the Jacobian of the system of equations. The Jacobian is a matrix whose rows are the gradients of the target functions. Alternatively, the method lets you supply the gradients of individual target functions as an array of either multivariate function returning a vector or multivariate function returning a vector in its second argument delegates.

The starting point for the iteration is set through the property. This property must be set to a valid before the algorithm is run. The and properties set the desired precision as specified by the property. The default value for both tolerances is (roughly 10-8). sets the maximum number of iterations, while sets the maximum number of function evaluations.
The method performs the actual approximation of the solution. This method returns the best approximation that was found. The property indicates whether the algorithm was successful.

The algorithm has two convergence tests. By default, the algorithm terminates when either of these is satisfied. You can deactivate either test by setting its property to . If both tests are deactivated, then the algorithm always terminates when the maximum number of iterations or function evaluations is reached.

The first test is based on the uncertainty in the location of the approximate solution. The property returns a object that allows you to specify the desired and specific . See the class for details on how to further customize this test.

The second test is based on the value of the target functions at the approximate solution. The property returns a object that can be used to customize the test. By default, the error is set to the component with the largest absolute value.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.EquationSolvers.RegulaFalsiSolver
member.summary: Represents a root finder that uses a modified regula falsi or false position algorithm.

remarks.para: The regula falsi method, also called the method of false position, is a root bracketing algorithm. It works by approximating the target function by a line. The bracketing interval is divided at the point where this line crosses the axis.

The regula falsi method is superior to the bisection method in that it will, in most cases, converge faster. However, in certain situations it can get 'stuck,' and convergence may actually be slower than the bisection method.
The Dekker-Brent method, and a further refinement implemented by the class, combine the best of both worlds.

inherits from , which in turn inherits from . All properties of are available. The and properties set the desired precision as specified by the property. The default value for both tolerances is (roughly 10-8). sets the maximum number of iterations.

The property is a function of one variable that specifies the function we want to find a root for. The and
properties specify the bounds of the bracketing interval. The target function must have a different sign at each end of this interval.

The method performs the actual approximation of the root. This method returns the best approximation that was found. The property indicates whether the algorithm was successful. The property gives an upper bound for the difference between the approximated and the actual root.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.EquationSolvers.RobustSolver
member.summary: Represents a root finder that uses an algorithm by Alefeld, Potra, and Shi.

remarks.para: Use the class to find a root of a function if you have an interval that includes a root with certainty. This is the most robust of the root bracketing solver algorithms.

inherits from , which in turn inherits from . All properties of are available. The and properties set the desired precision as specified by the property. The default value for both tolerances is (roughly 10-8). sets the maximum number of iterations.

The property is a function of one variable that specifies the function we want to find a root for. The and
properties specify the bounds of the bracketing interval. The target function must have a different sign at each end of this interval.

The method performs the actual approximation of the root. This method returns the best approximation that was found. The property indicates whether the algorithm was successful. The property gives an upper bound for the difference between the approximated and the actual root.

This method is a refinement of the Dekker-Brent method which for decades was the most advanced of the root bracketing algorithms. It combines the robustness of the bisection method with the increased speed of the regula falsi method.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.EquationSolvers.RootBracketingSolver
member.summary: Represents the abstract base class for root finders for real functions of one variable that use root bracketing.

remarks.para: When two points are known where the target function has different signs, the target function has a root in the interval between the two points, provided the target function is continuous.
Root bracketing root finders use this property by generating smaller and smaller intervals until the length of the interval is smaller than the requested tolerance.

item.description: Iteratively bisects the current bracketing interval and proceeds with the subinterval that still brackets the root.
Determines a new interval by approximating the target function by a line. The bracketing interval is divided at the point where this line crosses the X-axis.
Uses a combination of bi-section and inverse quadratic interpolation. This is one of the fastest and most reliable methods.
Uses a combination of bi-section, inverse quadratic, and inverse cubic interpolation. This is usually the fastest and most reliable method.

remarks.para: is an abstract class that cannot be instantiated directly. Use one of the derived classes instead.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.BandMatrix`1.ToGeneralBandMatrix
member.summary: Makes a copy of this instance and returns it as a general band matrix.
member.returns: A that is a copy of this instance.

remarks.para: The method converts a symmetric band matrix into a general band matrix. Only the components on and above the main diagonal of a symmetric band matrix are stored. This method constructs a band matrix that also stores the components below the main diagonal.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.BandMatrix`1.ToGeneralBandMatrix(System.Boolean)
member.summary: Makes a copy of this instance and returns it as a general band matrix.
member.param: A that indicates whether to allocate extra storage for a subsequent LU decomposition.
member.returns: A that is a copy of this instance.

remarks.para: This method has two primary uses. The first is to convert a symmetric band matrix into a general band matrix. Only the components on and above the main diagonal of a symmetric band matrix are stored. This method constructs a band matrix that also stores the components below the main diagonal.

The second use is to create a matrix suitable for computing an LU decomposition. The upper triangular part of an LU decomposition has a larger bandwidth than the original matrix. In order to calculate the LU decomposition, sufficient space must be allocated for these extra nonzero components.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.CholeskyDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the Cholesky decomposition of a positive-definite symmetric matrix.

remarks.para: The Cholesky decomposition of a real symmetric positive definite matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A= LLT, where L is a lower-triangular matrix.

can operate in two modes. In overwrite mode, the original matrix is overwritten with the result of the decomposition. In preserve mode, the original matrix is preserved, and a new matrix is created to hold the decomposition. You can set the mode through the property.

inherits from . This means you can use it to solve systems of linear equations where the matrix of the system is symmetric and positive definite. You can solve for a single right-hand side, or for multiple right-hand sides using the method. You can also calculate the determinant the inverse, and an estimate for the condition number.
To solve a general (non-symmetric or non-positive definite)system of equations, use the class instead.

The decomposition isn't performed until it is needed. You can force the calculation to take place by calling the method.

member.summary: Performs the actual Cholesky decomposition.

remarks.para: The decomposition isn't calculated until it is needed. When needed, it is called automatically. You never have to call explicitly unless you want to control when the decomposition is performed.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.CholeskyDecomposition`1.EstimateConditionNumber
member.summary: Calculates an estimate for the condition number of the decomposed dense matrix.
member.returns: An estimate for the condition number of the .

remarks.para: The condition number of a matrix is defined as the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value. Because the calculation of singular values is a very expensive operation, an estimate that is cheaper to calculate is usually preferred.
The condition number gives an indication of the worst case loss of precision when solving a system of simultaneous linear equations.
The condition number of a singular matrix is infinite.
This method uses the LAPACK routine ?POCON.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.ComplexSingularValueDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the singular value decomposition of a matrix.

remarks.para: The singular value decomposition (SVD) of a matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A= USVT, where U and V are orthogonal matrices, and S is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal contains the singular values of the matrix.

can operate in two modes. In overwrite mode, the original matrix is overwritten by the decomposition. In preserve mode, the original matrix is preserved, and a new matrix is created to hold the decomposition. You can set the mode through the property.

inherits from . This means you can use it to solve systems of linear equations. You can solve for a single right-hand side, or for multiple right-hand sides using the method. You can also calculate the determinant, the inverse, and an estimate for the .
In addition, the class provides some unique methods. The method calculates the pseudo-inverse of the matrix. This is a matrix A+ such that AA+A = A.
The managed implementation of the singular value decomposition is based on the LINPACK routine DSVDC. The native version uses the LAPACK routine ?GESDD.

remarks.para: A system of simultaneous linear equations has a unique solution if its determinant is not equal to zero.
Determinants are only defined for square matrices. If the matrix is not square, an exception of type is thrown.

For a singular value decomposition A = USVT, the magnitude of the determinant is the product of the diagonal elements of S. Since U and V are orthogonal, the modulus of their determinant is 1. This means that only the magnitude of the determinant is known.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.ComponentReadOnlyException
member.summary: Represents an exception that is thrown when an attempt is made to set a component of a or whose value is fixed.

remarks.para: Many matrices have a clearly defined structure. For example, all elements above the diagonal of a lower triangular matrix are zero. If the matrix is also unit diagonal, then its diagonal elements have the fixed value of 1.
Changing the value of one of these elements would cause the vector or matrix to lose its structure. This is not allowed. If an attempt is made to do so, a is thrown.

You can verify whether a component of a vector is writable by calling its method. You can verify whether a component of a matrix is writable by calling its method. These methods return if the component is read-only, and a would be thrown if an attempt was made to change its value.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.ComposedComplexVector`1
member.summary: Represents a complex vector composed of a vector of real and of imaginary components.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent a complex vector where the real and imaginary parts are stored in separate, real vectors. If the imaginary components are not defined, they are assumed to be zero. This makes this class especially useful for storing a real matrix as a complex matrix.
The class provides methods and properties for all the common operations on vectors, including norms, dot products, as well as retrieving extreme values from a vector.
Overloaded versions of the major arithmetic operators are provided for languages that support them. For languages that don't support operator overloading, equivalent methods are supplied.
To allow for greater efficiency, overloaded instance methods are available for many compound operations on vectors.

member.summary: Calculates an estimate for the condition number of this matrix.
member.returns: An estimate for the condition number of the .

remarks.para: The condition number of a matrix is defined as the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value. For a diagonal matrix, the condition number is very easy to calculate. The condition number of a singular matrix is infinite.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.Decomposition`1
member.summary: Represents a matrix decomposition.

remarks.para: The class represents a decomposition of a matrix into a product of matrices with specific properties.

The class defines methods and properties that are shared by all decomposition classes. This includes methods related to solving systems of simultaneous linear equations defined by the abstract base class.

The class is an abstract base class and cannot be instantiated directly. Instead, use one of its derived classes. These are: ClassDescription
Represents a decomposition into a lower and an upper-triangular matrix.
Represents a decomposition into an orthogonal and an upper triangular matrix.
Represents the decomposition of a into the product of a lower-triangular matrix and its transpose..
Notes to inheritors: When you inherit from , you must override the following members: , , , , .

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.DenseMatrix`1
member.summary: Represents a general, dense, square or rectangular matrix.
member.typeparam: The type of the elements of the matrix.

remarks.para: A matrix is a two-dimensional array of real numbers. Use the class to represent general, dense matrices. It is the most general implementation of the class. No components are assumed to have a specific value, and no relationship is assumed to exist between different components.

The components of a are stored in a one-dimensional array of values. By default, components that are adjacent in a column of the matrix are adjacent in the storage array. The components are said to be stored in column major order. It is also possible to have elements stored in row major order.

The class implements algorithms using the general matrix BLAS and LAPACK routines. These routines assume matrix components are stored in column major order. However, any necessary conversions are performed transparently. No additional work is needed. In some cases there might be a small performance penalty.
Because can represent any matrix, it is often used as the return type of matrix operations.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.DenseVector`1
member.summary: Represents a vector with arbitrary components.

remarks.para: The class represents a one-dimensional array of real numbers.
The class provides methods and properties for all the common operations on vectors, including norms, as well as retrieving extreme values from a vector.
Overloaded versions of the major arithmetic operators are provided for languages that support them. For languages that don't support operator overloading, equivalent methods are supplied.
To allow for greater efficiency, overloaded instance methods are available for many compound operations on vectors.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.DenseVector`2
member.summary: Represents a vector with arbitrary components.

remarks.para: The class represents a one-dimensional array of real numbers.
The class provides methods and properties for all the common operations on vectors, including norms, dot products, as well as retrieving extreme values from a vector.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.EigenvalueDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the eigenvalue decomposition of a dense matrix.

remarks.para: The eigenvalue decomposition of a real square matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A= XLX-1, where X is a matrix and L is a diagonal matrix. The diagonal elements of L are the eigenvalues. The columns of X are the corresponding eigenvectors.

The eigenvalues are either real or come in complex conjugate pairs. The eigenvectors corresponding to real eigenvalues are also real. The eigenvectors corresponding to pairs of complex conjugate eigenvalues are themselves complex conjugates.

The eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are always real, and its eigenvectors are orthogonal. Its eigenvalue decomposition can be calculated more easily. Likewise, the eigenvalues of a complex Hermitian matrix are also real.

inherits from . However, unlike the other decompositions, the eigenvalue decomposition does not offer a speed advantage when performing most calculations. For example, solving an equation using the eigenvalue decomposition itself requires the solution of a system of equations. For this reason, the , and and similar methods methods simply call the corresponding method on the base matrix.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.GeneralizedEigenvalueDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the generalized eigenvalue decomposition of two matrices.

remarks.para: The eigenvalue decomposition of a pair of square matrices A and B computes scalars ?,? and vectors x, y so that
Ax = ?Bx.
or
?Ay = By.

The scalars are called (generalized) eigenvalues and the vectors are called eigenvectors. If neither ? nor ? is zero, then the two problems are equivalent with x=y and ?=1/?. To cover the case where either may be zero or very small, two sets of values are returned, so that the eigenvalues are equal to their quotient.

The eigenvalues are either real or come in complex conjugate pairs. The eigenvectors corresponding to real eigenvalues are also real. The eigenvectors corresponding to pairs of complex conjugate eigenvalues are themselves complex conjugates.

The generalized eigenvalues of a pair of real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrices where the secondary matrix is positive definite are always real,and its eigenvectors are orthogonal with respect to the second matrix. Its eigenvalue decomposition can be calculated more easily.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.GeneralizedSchurDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the generalized Schur decomposition of two square matrices.

remarks.para: The generalized Schur decomposition or QZ decomposition of a pair of square matrices A and B computes orthogonal (unitary) matrices, Q and Z, so that
A = QSZ* and B = QTZ*.
where S and T are upper triangular matrices.
The matrices S and T are called the Schur forms of A and B, respectively. The rows of the matrices Q and Z are called the left and right Schur vectors.
The generalized eigenvalues of A and B are the ratios of corresponding diagonal elements of S and T.

For a real matrix, the generalized eigenvalues are either real or come in complex conjugate pairs. When there are complex eigenvalues, the matrix S is modified to be quasi-triangular, where 2x2 blocks on the diagonal correspond to the complex eigenvalues. This is called the real Schur form. The matrix T is always upper triangular.
inherits from.

A = U Σ1 [0 R] QT
B = V Σ2 [0 R] QT.
where U, V, and Q are orthogonal matrices (unitary if is complex), Σ1 and Σ2 are real diagonal matrices, and R is an upper triangular matrix.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.HermitianMatrix`1
member.summary: Represents a matrix that is Hermitian about the main diagonal.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent dense matrices whose elements are Hermitian about the main diagonal. Hermitian matrices are always square.
The components of a are stored in a one-dimensional array of values. Thanks to the symmetry, only the upper or lower-triangular portion needs to be stored.
Hermitian matrices can be constructed from scratch, or they can be derived or extracted from the upper or lower triangular portion of a using one of the methods.
The class implements algorithms using the Hermitian matrix BLAS and LAPACK routines. Hermitian matrices are always stored in column-major order.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.HermitianMatrix`1.EstimateConditionNumber
member.summary: Calculates an estimate for the condition number of the Hermitian matrix.
member.returns: An estimate for the condition number of the .

remarks.para: The condition number of a matrix is defined as the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value. Because the calculation of singular values is a very expensive operation, an estimate that is cheaper to calculate is usually preferred.
The condition number gives an indication of the worst case loss of precision when solving a system of simultaneous linear equations.
The condition number of a singular matrix is infinite.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.LeastSquaresSolver`1
member.summary: Represents the solution to a least squares problem.

remarks.para: Use the class to compute the least squares solution of a system of equations. When a system of linear equations is over-determined, an exact solution may not exist. The least squares solution is the vector that minimizes the sum of the squares of the residuals. To make sure the solution is uniquely defined, the solution with the smallest norm is returned.

The coefficient matrix and the right-hand side must be specified in the constructor. Several methods are available to compute the solution. These can be selected through the property. This is a value. The default is to use a QR decomposition. For ill-conditioned problems, it may be better to use a singular value decomposition. If speed is the dominant factor, then the method using the normal equations is the fastest, at the expense of some accuracy.

A non-negative least squares solution is restricted by having only positive or zero entries in the solution. To compute the non-negative least squares solution, select the value NonNegative for the solution method.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.LeastSquaresSolver`1.#ctor(Numerics.NET.Matrix{`0},Numerics.NET.Vector{`0})
member.summary: Constructs a new from the matrix of observations and the vector of outcomes.
member.param: A whose rows contain the observations of the least squares problem.
A vector containing the outcomes of each of the observations in .

remarks.para: Use this constructor to create a least squares solution based on the matrix of observations and the vector of outcomes. The number of rows in must equal the number of elements in . In addition, the number of rows in must be greater than or equal to the number of columns.
Each row in the matrix corresponds to an observation. The corresponding element of the vector specifies the outcome produced by this observation.

Because there are at least as many equations as there are unknowns, an exact solution is not possible. The goal is therefore to minimize the two-norm of the residual vector Ax - b, where A corresponds to and b corresponds to . The vector x with this property is the solution to this problem with minimal norm.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.LinearOperator`1
member.summary: Defines methods for the solution of a system of simultaneous linear equations and related operations.

remarks.para: is implemented by all classes and all classes that represent matrix decompositions.

The solution of a system of simultaneous linear equations represented by a is one of the most common tasks in linear algebra. The mechanism, which is overloaded, defines a common method for all classes that can represent matrices. This not only includes the class and its descendants, but also the class and its descendants.
also defines operations that are related to solving systems of equations, such as calculating the matrix , the and an estimate for the .

member.summary: Calculates an estimate for the condition number of a matrix.
member.returns: An estimate for the condition number of the matrix.

remarks.para: The condition number of a matrix is defined as the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value. Because the calculation of singular values is a very expensive operation, an estimate that is cheaper to calculate is usually preferred.
The condition number gives an indication of the worst case loss of precision when solving a system of simultaneous linear equations.
The condition number of a singular matrix is infinite.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.LQDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the LQ decomposition of a matrix.

remarks.para: The LQ decomposition of a matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A= LQ, where Q is an orthogonal matrix, and L is a lower-triangular matrix.
The class has no constructors. Instead, use the instance method to create an LQ decomposition for a matrix.

can operate in two modes. In overwrite mode, the original matrix is overwritten by the decomposition. In preserve mode, the original matrix is preserved, and a new matrix is created to hold the decomposition. You can set the mode through the property.

inherits from . This means you can use it to solve systems of linear equations. You can solve for a single right-hand side, or for multiple right-hand sides using the method. You can also calculate the determinant, the inverse, and an estimate for the .

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.LQDecomposition`1.#ctor(Numerics.NET.Matrix{`0},System.Boolean)
member.summary: Constructs a new .
member.param: The matrix that is to be decomposed.
If , the matrix is preserved. (This is the default.) If , is destroyed by the decomposition.

remarks.para: The decomposition isn't performed until it is needed. You can force the calculation to take place by calling the method.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.LQDecomposition`1.Decompose
member.summary: Calculates the actual LQ decomposition.

remarks.para: The decomposition isn't calculated until it is needed. When needed, it is called automatically. You never have to call explicitly unless you want to control when the decomposition is performed.
Until is called, either explicitly or implicitly by one of its methods or properties, you can set the property to specify whether to overwrite or preserve the original matrix.

The lower triangular factor R.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.LQDecomposition`1.EstimateConditionNumber
member.summary: Calculates an estimate for the condition number of the matrix.
member.returns: An estimate for the condition number of the .

remarks.para: The condition number of a matrix is defined as the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value. Because the calculation of singular values is a very expensive operation, an estimate that is cheaper to calculate is usually preferred.
The condition number gives an indication of the worst case loss of precision when solving a system of simultaneous linear equations.
The condition number of a singular matrix is infinite.

member.summary: Gets a collection of the matrix factors that make up the decomposition.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.LQDecomposition`1.GetDeterminant
member.summary: Calculates the determinant of the decomposed matrix.
member.returns: The determinant of the matrix.

remarks.para: A system of simultaneous linear equations has a unique solution if its determinant is not equal to zero.
Determinants are only defined for square matrices. If the matrix is not square, an exception of type is thrown.
For a LQ factorized matrix A = LQ, the magnitude of the determinant is the product of the diagonal elements of R. Since Q is orthogonal, its determinant is 1 or -1.

member.summary: Calculates the inverse of the factorized matrix.
member.returns: A that is the matrix inverse of this instance.

remarks.para: The inverse of a matrix is the matrix that, when multiplied by the original matrix, gives an identity matrix.
If the matrix is singular, its inverse does not exist and a is thrown.
The inverse is only defined for a square matrix. If the matrix is not square, an exception of type is thrown.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.NonHermitianEigenvalueDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the eigenvalue decomposition of a complex matrix.

remarks.para: The eigenvalue decomposition of a real square general matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A= XLX-1, where X is a matrix and L is a diagonal matrix. The diagonal elements of L are the eigenvalues. The columns of X are the corresponding eigenvectors.

The eigenvalues are either real or come in complex conjugate pairs. The eigenvectors corresponding to real eigenvalues are also real. The eigenvectors corresponding to pairs of complex conjugate eigenvalues are themselves complex conjugates.
The eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are always real, and its eigenvectors are orthogonal. Its eigenvalue decomposition can be calculated more easily.

inherits from . However, unlike the other decompositions, the non-symmetric eigenvalue decomposition does not offer a speed advantage when performing calculations most calculations. For example, solving an equation using the eigen decomposition itself requires the solution of a system of equations. For this reason, the , and
methods simply call the corresponding method on the base matrix.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.NonNegativeMatrixFactorization`1
member.summary: Represents a non-negative decomposition of a general matrix.

remarks.para: Use the class to compute an approximate factorization of a into matrices with only positive components. In other words, it rewrites a matrix X as a product
X = WH.

where W and H have only zero or positive components. The inner dimension of the product (the number of columns of W and the number of rows of H) may be less than the rank of X. In this case, the factorization is only an approximation to the original matrix. This is actually very common, since the Non-Negative Matrix Factorization is often used to reduce the dimensionality of data.

The constructor takes two arguments. The first is the matrix that is to be factorized. The second is the inner dimension of the product. The method performs the actual calculation using an alternating least squares method. The resulting factors are then available as the and properties.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.RealEigenvalueDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the eigenvalue decomposition of a non-symmetric, real matrix.

remarks.para: Use the class to get access to properties specific to the eigenvalue decomposition of a real, square matrix.

The eigenvalue decomposition of a real square general matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A = XLX-1, where X is a matrix and L is a diagonal matrix. The diagonal elements of L are the eigenvalues. The columns of X are the corresponding eigenvectors.

The eigenvalues are either real or come in complex conjugate pairs. The eigenvectors corresponding to real eigenvalues are also real. The eigenvectors corresponding to pairs of complex conjugate eigenvalues are themselves complex conjugates. The and properties return only the real eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The and properties return the full set of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The property returns the real and imaginary parts of all eigenvectors.

The eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are always real, and its eigenvectors are real and orthogonal. Its eigenvalue decomposition can be calculated more easily, and there is no need to allow for complex eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

inherits from . However, unlike the other decompositions, the non-symmetric eigenvalue decomposition does not offer a speed advantage when performing calculations most calculations. For example, solving an equation using the eigen decomposition itself requires the solution of a system of equations. For this reason, the , and methods simply call the corresponding method on the base matrix.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.SchurDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the Schur decomposition of a dense matrix.

remarks.para: The Schur decomposition of a real (complex) square matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A= QTQ*, where Q is an orthogonal (unitary) matrix and T, the Schur form, is an upper triangular matrix. The diagonal elements of T are the eigenvalues of A.

For a real matrix, the eigenvalues are either real or come in complex conjugate pairs. When there are complex eigenvalues, the matrix T is modified to be quasi-triangular, where 2x2 blocks on the diagonal indicate complex conjugate pairs of eigenvalues. This is sometimes referred to as the real Schur form.
The Schur form of a complex matrix is always upper triangular.
The Schur form of a real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrix is a diagonal matrix. Therefore, the Schur decomposition of such a matrix is the same as the eigenvalue decomposition.

inherits from . However, unlike most other decompositions, the Schur decomposition does not offer a speed advantage when performing most calculations. For example, solving an equation using the eigenvalue decomposition itself requires the solution of a system of equations. For this reason, the , and and similar methods simply call the corresponding method on the base matrix.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.SingularValueDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the singular value decomposition of a matrix.

remarks.para: The singular value decomposition (SVD) of a matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A= USVT, where U and V are orthogonal matrices, and S is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal contains the singular values of the matrix.

can operate in two modes. In overwrite mode, the original matrix is overwritten by the decomposition. In preserve mode, the original matrix is preserved, and a new matrix is created to hold the decomposition. You can set the mode through the property.

inherits from . This means you can use it to solve systems of linear equations. You can solve for a single right-hand side, or for multiple right-hand sides using the method. You can also calculate the determinant, the inverse, and an estimate for the .
In addition, the class provides some unique methods. The method calculates the pseudo-inverse of the matrix. This is a matrix A+ such that AA+A = A.
The managed implementation of the singular value decomposition is based on the LINPACK routine DSVDC. The native version uses the LAPACK routine ?GESDD.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.SparseCompressedColumnMatrix`1
member.summary: Represents a sparse matrix in Compressed Sparse Column format.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent sparse matrices. Only the nonzero elements of the matrix are stored. This not only saves memory, but also allows many calculations to be performed faster.
The compressed sparse column format stores the components in column-major order. Within each column, only the row indexes and the values of the nonzero components are stored.

The components of a sparse matrix can be specified in a variety of ways. A common method is to supply the rows, columns, and values of the nonzero components. Another way is to build up the matrix using the Insert methods: , , , , . Individual components can also be set, but this is generally less efficient.
Sparse matrices can also be read directly from values files in Matrix Market format.

The property returns the number of nonzero components. The property returns a number between 0 and 1 that is the proportion of nonzero components to the total number of components in the matrix. To iterate through the nonzero components of a sparse matrix, use the property. This property enumerates objects, each containing the row, column, and value of a nonzero component.

A disadvantage of sparse matrices is that working with individual components tends to be slower. Every access usually requires a lookup in a list. To avoid duplicate lookups for elementary operations on components, use one of the specialized methods: , , and .

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.SymmetricIndefiniteDecomposition`1
member.summary: Represents the symmetric indefinite (Bunch-Kaufman) decomposition of a symmetric matrix.

remarks.para: The Bunch-Kaufman decomposition of a real symmetric positive definite matrix A rewrites the matrix in the form A= LDLT or A= UDUT, where L is a unit lower triangular matrix, U is an unit upper triangular matrix, and D is a block diagonal matrix made up of 1x1 and 2x2 blocks.

can operate in two modes. In overwrite mode, the original matrix is overwritten with the result of the decomposition. In preserve mode, the original matrix is preserved, and a new matrix is created to hold the decomposition. You can set the mode through the property.

inherits from . This means you can use it to solve systems of linear equations where the matrix of the system is symmetric but not necessarily. You can solve for a single right-hand side, or for multiple right-hand sides using the method. You can also calculate the determinant the inverse, and an estimate for the condition number.
To solve a symmetric positive definite system of equations, you can use the class instead.

member.summary: Constructs a new object.
member.param: The that is to be factorized. This matrix must be positive-definite, or the decomposition will fail.
If , the matrix is preserved. (This is the default.) If , is destroyed by the decomposition.

remarks.para: By default, the matrix is preserved. It may be more efficient to overwrite the components of with the result of the decomposition. To do this, set the property to immediately after creating the .
The decomposition isn't performed until it is needed. You can force the calculation to take place by calling the method.

member.summary: Returns the numerical rank of the matrix using the specified tolerance.
member.param: The absolute tolerance used to determine if a matrix component is considered zero.

remarks.para: If is negative, the default tolerance is used. The rank is determined by counting the number of diagonal elements of the triangular component of the decomposition whose absolute value is greater than the tolerance.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.SymmetricMatrix`1
member.summary: Represents a matrix that is symmetrical about the main diagonal.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent dense matrices whose elements are symmetrical about the main diagonal. Symmetric matrices are always square.
The elements of a are stored in a one-dimensional array of values. Thanks to the symmetry, only the upper or lower-triangular portion needs to be stored.

Symmetric matrices can be constructed from scratch, or they can be derived or extracted from the upper or lower triangular portion of a using one of the
methods.
The class implements algorithms using the symmetric matrix BLAS and LAPACK routines. Symmetric matrices are always stored in column-major order.

member.summary: Calculates an estimate for the condition number of the symmetric matrix.
member.returns: An estimate for the condition number of the .

remarks.para: The condition number of a matrix is defined as the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value. Because the calculation of singular values is a very expensive operation, an estimate that is cheaper to calculate is usually preferred.
The condition number gives an indication of the worst case loss of precision when solving a system of simultaneous linear equations.
The condition number of a singular matrix is infinite.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.TriangularMatrix`1
member.summary: Represents a matrix whose elements above or below the main diagonal are zero.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent dense matrices whose elements above or below the diagonal are zero. The name is derived from the shape of the non-zero elements, which form a triangle. However, this class also represents rectangular matrices, whose non-zero elements may form a trapezoid.
A can be either upper or lower-triangular, depending on which components are non-zero. This property is available as the property. It is of type , and must be specified at construction.

Sometimes, the components on the diagonal are all equal to one. In this case, the matrix is said to be unit-diagonal, and the property will be . Once again, this must be specified at the time the matrix is constructed.

Only the non-zero components of a triangular matrix can be modified. The diagonal components of a unit-diagonal matrix can't be modified. An attempt to do so will result in an . You can verify if a component can be modified by calling the method.

The components of a are stored in a one-dimensional array of values. By default, components that are adjacent in a column of the matrix are adjacent in the storage array. The components are said to be stored in column major order. It is also possible to have elements stored in row major order.
Triangular matrices can be constructed from scratch, or they can be derived or extracted from a using one of the or methods.
The rows and column vectors of a triangular matrix are of type .

The class implements algorithms using the triangular matrix BLAS and LAPACK routines. These routines assume matrix components are stored in column major order. However, any necessary conversions are performed transparently. No additional work is needed. In some cases there might be a small performance penalty.
objects are used as properties of many matrix decompositions. Both factors of the LU decomposition are triangular. So is at least one factor of the Cholesky Decomposition and the QR Decomposition.

member.name: M:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.TriangularMatrix`1.EstimateConditionNumber
member.summary: Calculates an estimate for the condition number of this .
member.returns: An estimate for the condition number of the .

remarks.para: The condition number of a matrix is defined as the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value. Because the calculation of singular values is a very expensive operation, an estimate that is cheaper to calculate is usually preferred.
The condition number gives an indication of the worst case loss of precision when solving a system of simultaneous linear equations.
The condition number of a singular matrix is infinite.

member.summary: Represents a Vandermonde matrix.
member.typeparam: The type of the elements of the matrix.

remarks.para: Use the class to represent a Vandermonde matrix or its transpose. A Vandermonde matrix is a matrix whose rows are rising powers of a set of values, starting with exponent zero.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.Implementation.DecompositionOperations`1
member.summary: Specifies the methods that must be implemented by a class to support real LAPACK routines for general matrices.

remarks.para: The Linear Algebra PACKage (LAPACK) is the de facto standard for more complex linear algebra problems. It complements the Basic Linear Algebra Subroutines (BLAS), which defines standards for low level vector and matrix operations.

member.name: T:Numerics.NET.LinearAlgebra.Implementation.DecompositionOperations`2
member.summary: Specifies the methods that must be implemented by a class to support complex LAPACK routines for general matrices.

remarks.para: The Linear Algebra PACKage (LAPACK) is the de facto standard for more complex linear algebra problems. It complements the Basic Linear Algebra Subroutines (BLAS), which defines standards for low level vector and matrix operations.

summary.para: Computes the Cholesky factorization of a complex Hermitian positive definite band matrix A.

param.name: uplo
param.pre: = 'U': Upper triangle of A is stored; = 'L': Lower triangle of A is stored.

param.name: n
param.pre: The order of the matrix A. N >= 0.

param.name: kd
param.pre: The number of superdiagonals of the matrix A if UPLO = 'U', or the number of subdiagonals if UPLO = 'L'. KD >= 0.

param.name: ab
param.pre: AB is array, dimension (LDAB,N) On entry, the upper or lower triangle of the Hermitian band matrix A, stored in the first KD+1 rows of the array. The j-th column of A is stored in the j-th column of the array AB as follows: if UPLO = 'U', AB(kd+1+i-j,j) = A(i,j) for max(1,j-kd)<=i<=j; if UPLO = 'L', AB(1+i-j,j) = A(i,j) for j<=i<=min(n,j+kd). On exit, if INFO = 0, the triangular factor U or L from the Cholesky factorization A = UH*U or A = L*LH of the band matrix A, in the same storage format as A.
The leading dimension of the array AB. LDAB >= KD+1.

param.name: info
param.pre: = 0: successful exit < 0: if INFO = -i, the i-th argument had an illegal value > 0: if INFO = i, the leading minor of order i is not positive definite, and the factorization could not be completed.

para.pre: The factorization has the form A = UH * U, if UPLO = 'U', or A = L * LH, if UPLO = 'L', where U is an upper triangular matrix and L is lower triangular.

The band storage scheme is illustrated by the following example, when N = 6, KD = 2, and UPLO = 'U': On entry: On exit: * * a13 a24 a35 a46 * * u13 u24 u35 u46 * a12 a23 a34 a45 a56 * u12 u23 u34 u45 u56 a11 a22 a33 a44 a55 a66 u11 u22 u33 u44 u55 u66 Similarly, if UPLO = 'L' the format of A is as follows: On entry: On exit: a11 a22 a33 a44 a55 a66 l11 l22 l33 l44 l55 l66 a21 a32 a43 a54 a65 * l21 l32 l43 l54 l65 * a31 a42 a53 a64 * * l31 l42 l53 l64 * * Array elements marked * are not used by the routine.

remarks.para: Peter Mayes and Giuseppe Radicati, IBM ECSEC, Rome, March 23, 1989
Authors: Univ. of Tennessee, Univ. of California Berkeley, Univ. of Colorado Denver, NAG Ltd.
Date: November 2011

summary.para: Computes the Cholesky factorization of a real symmetric positive definite band matrix A.

param.name: storedTriangle
param.pre: = 'U': Upper triangle of A is stored; = 'L': Lower triangle of A is stored.

param.name: n
param.pre: The order of the matrix A. N >= 0.

param.name: kd
param.pre: The number of superdiagonals of the matrix A if UPLO = 'U', or the number of subdiagonals if UPLO = 'L'. KD >= 0.

param.name: ab
param.pre: AB is array, dimension (LDAB,N) On entry, the upper or lower triangle of the symmetric band matrix A, stored in the first KD+1 rows of the array. The j-th column of A is stored in the j-th column of the array AB as follows: if UPLO = 'U', AB(kd+1+i-j,j) = A(i,j) for max(1,j-kd)<=i<=j; if UPLO = 'L', AB(1+i-j,j) = A(i,j) for j<=i<=min(n,j+kd). On exit, if INFO = 0, the triangular factor U or L from the Cholesky factorization A = UT*U or A = L*LT of the band matrix A, in the same storage format as A.
The leading dimension of the array AB. LDAB >= KD+1.

param.name: info

summary.para: Estimates the reciprocal of the condition number (in the 1-norm) of a complex Hermitian positive definite band matrix using the Cholesky factorization A = UH*U or A = L*LH computed by ZPBTRF.

param.name: uplo
param.pre: = 'U': Upper triangular factor stored in AB; = 'L': Lower triangular factor stored in AB.

param.name: n
param.pre: The order of the matrix A. N >= 0.

param.name: kd
param.pre: The number of superdiagonals of the matrix A if UPLO = 'U', or the number of sub-diagonals if UPLO = 'L'. KD >= 0.

param.name: ab
param.pre: AB is array, dimension (LDAB,N) The triangular factor U or L from the Cholesky factorization A = UH*U or A = L*LH of the band matrix A, stored in the first KD+1 rows of the array. The j-th column of U or L is stored in the j-th column of the array AB as follows: if UPLO ='U', AB(kd+1+i-j,j) = U(i,j) for max(1,j-kd)<=i<=j; if UPLO ='L', AB(1+i-j,j) = L(i,j) for j<=i<=min(n,j+kd).
The leading dimension of the array AB. LDAB >= KD+1.

param.name: anorm
param.pre: ANORM is The 1-norm (or infinity-norm) of the Hermitian band matrix A.

param.name: rcond
param.pre: RCOND is The reciprocal of the condition number of the matrix A, computed as RCOND = 1/(ANORM * AINVNM), where AINVNM is an estimate of the 1-norm of inv(A) computed in this routine.

param.name: info
param.pre: = 0: successful exit < 0: if INFO = -i, the i-th argument had an illegal value

para.pre: An estimate is obtained for norm(inv(A)), and the reciprocal of the condition number is computed as RCOND = 1 / (ANORM * norm(inv(A))).
